title: Before adding latent variables: what scale building and path analysis can do
text:
The previous article, “From survey items to a scale, then on to regression and QCA: a step-by-step guide,” described a path from several survey items through factor analysis, Cronbach’s alpha, and subscale scores to regression analysis. This article is its sequel.
For some time, graduate students and other researchers have asked me the same kind of question: “If we are working with constructs, shouldn’t we use SEM with latent variables (rather than regression or path analysis) instead of first building factor scores or subscales through factor analysis?” Sometimes the question comes from someone who understands the mathematics. In what I have seen and heard, however, a common reason is a non-essential one, such as “SEM looks cooler” (a person who really understands SEM would not ask the question in the first place). I also hear of cases where, in graduate supervision, a student was simply told, “Let’s go with SEM (with latent variables) for now.”
This article is my own answer to that question. My position can be summarized in one point.
Of course, this does not mean “do not use models with latent variables.” It means that if you use one, you should be able to explain in your own words why you are using it. The more advanced the method, the more serious a mistake made without understanding the reasoning tends to be.
If you do not include latent variables and use subscale scores instead, the measurement error contained in the scores can make the coefficients in the structural part smaller than they should be, or biased. I am aware of this. I still recommend that beginners start with scale building. The reason is that adding latent variables increases the assumptions, the judgments, and the responsibility in estimation, and that using such a model without being able to explain these brings a different kind of problem. I do acknowledge that a latent-variable model is one answer to the problem of measurement error. What I would like readers to do is check, against their own research question, whether that answer is needed (Question A in Section 4). That is the point of this article.
There are many opinions about how to use SEM. Please read every claim below as meaning “I (Toyoda) think that …”.

title: Before adding latent variables: what scale building and path analysis can do
section: 1. Terms: the issue is not “SEM or not”
text:
1. Terms: the issue is not “SEM or not”
First, let me align the terms. If they stay vague, the later discussion will not connect.
SEM (structural equation modeling) is the name of a broad framework that expresses and estimates the relations among several variables as one unified model. Several kinds of models belong to it.

Models with observed variables only (path analysis): These use only variables that were actually measured (including subscale scores built from them) and estimate the relations among them. (Multiple regression can be seen as a special case of path analysis.) In other words, path analysis is also part of SEM in the broad sense.
Models with latent variables: A construct that cannot be measured directly is placed in the model as a “latent variable,” and several observed items are assumed to measure it. The part of the model that links items to a latent variable is called the measurement model. When relations among latent variables are added, we also handle the structural model (the part that describes the relations among constructs).
Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) is one kind of latent-variable model. It contains latent variables, but it may have no structural model.

For this reason, I avoid the phrase “use SEM or not” in this article. Saying it invites the fair objection that path analysis is also a kind of SEM. The issue of this article is one point.

Whether to put latent variables into the model.

A method that builds scales in advance and then runs regression or path analysis with subscale scores does not put latent variables into the model. In this article I call it the “observed-variable model.” A method that does put latent variables in is called the “latent-variable model.”
Note that “not putting latent variables in” does not mean that factor analysis is not used when you examine a scale. Factor analysis itself is a latent-variable model. The article distinguishes two things. One is a method in which factor analysis and similar tools are used at the measurement stage to build a scale, and the resulting scores are then treated as observed variables in regression or path analysis. The other is a method in which the measurement model is built into the structural model, and the relations among latent variables are estimated.
In this article I also write “association” for the links between variables. Arrows in path analysis and regression coefficients do not show causal relations when the data are cross-sectional survey data (observational data). This is the same whether the model has latent variables or only observed variables.

title: Before adding latent variables: what scale building and path analysis can do
section: 2. Why does “latent variables for everything” happen so easily?
text:
2. Why does “latent variables for everything” happen so easily?
From what I have seen and heard, I think the reasons fall roughly into the following three (this is my observation, not the result of a survey).

Because you see it in papers. Academic papers often use models with latent variables. They look like “proper academic analysis,” so people want to imitate them.
Because you think that constructs exist. You are dealing with a concept such as “brand trust,” so making it a latent variable feels natural. But having a construct and using a latent variable in the analysis are different things. As the previous article explained, defining a construct first, measuring it with several items, checking reliability, and using subscale scores is also a way of taking constructs seriously.
Because software makes it easy. With software such as AMOS, you draw a diagram, press a button, and get results. (If you wrote out the structural equations, you would see the complexity, but drawing the model as a diagram makes it look simple.) Being able to run a model and being able to explain its results are different things.

None of these reasons comes from the research question. The method comes first. I would like the order to be the opposite: first the question, then the conditions of measurement, and only after that the choice of method.

title: Before adding latent variables: what scale building and path analysis can do
section: 3. What increases when latent variables are added?
text:
3. What increases when latent variables are added?
Adding latent variables increases the expressive power of the model. At the same time, the number of things you must judge yourself increases.

An analogy: think of arrows as springs
To understand models with latent variables intuitively, I use the following analogy (in lectures I sometimes say that the springs go “boing,” stretching and shrinking). It is only an image, not a rigorous explanation.
Think of each arrow in the model as a spring. Each spring represents a relation between variables. The strength of the spring is the estimate. When many springs are connected, changing the strength of one spring pulls on the others, and the whole system readjusts. The system then settles at a balanced position (the position where the computation settles). That position is the estimate that is finally reported.

  

Video 1: a model with observed variables only. The numbers and the motion are illustrative.
As the springs increase and tangle with one another, a poorly specified part at one place can pass its distortion on to the other springs, and the system can balance at an unexpected position. Because it is balanced, the result looks “settled and plausible.”
In real models, something close to this happens in the following forms.

When the specification of the structural part changes, the estimates in the measurement part can move too (interpretational confounding; Burt, 1976).
Estimation does not converge, or an improper solution such as a negative variance appears.
Other models of a different form fit equally well (equivalent models; MacCallum et al., 1993).

Let me separate three things here: “the computation settling (convergence),” “fitting the data well (fit),” and “being theoretically valid.” They are different things. Even if the springs are balanced and settled, that is not necessarily the right position. A model can converge and still fit poorly, and a model can fit well and still lack theoretical validity.
Limits of the analogy: Actual estimation is not a physical phenomenon in which springs sway and move. It is a computation that searches for numbers that make the gap between the data and the model as small as possible. Nor does “many springs” mean “a bad model.” Complex models are also powerful. The point of the analogy is that, as models become more complex, everything moves together, so it becomes harder to check by yourself where and what is happening.

Continuing the analogy: fixed points and invisible joints
Each spring has “points” at both ends. There are two kinds of points.

An observed variable is a fixed point whose position is set by the data. Its position does not move (this is an analogy, so it is an image).
A latent variable is an invisible joint that is not directly observed. Its position is not set by the data, so where to place it is also decided inside the model, while looking at the relations as a whole. (The “position” here is not a coordinate in real space. It is an image of how to place the cluster that appears in common across several items.)

If you only connect fixed points with springs, the points do not move, so mainly the strength of the springs changes. Even so, springs attached to the same point move together. If you remove or add one spring, the strength of other springs can also change.
Adding invisible joints changes the situation. Where the joint is placed and how strong the attached springs are must be decided at the same time, while looking at the whole. So when you change one connection, the placement of the invisible joint changes too, and the estimates of other relations attached to it can be affected. And because the joint is invisible, it becomes harder to confirm from the outside “where, and what, moved.”

  

Video 2: a model with a latent variable. The numbers and the motion are illustrative.
So how does the procedure of building a scale (“measurement”: factor analysis, alpha, subscale scores; see the previous article) look in this analogy? Building a subscale can be seen as a method that, instead of moving the invisible joint itself inside the model, creates a representative value from several items (the mean of the items) and treats it as one observed point (a fixed point). Before fixing it, we check whether the group of items is sensible, using factor analysis and alpha. After this check, we connect the fixed points with springs (regression or path analysis).
Connecting everything at once, with the invisible joints still included from the start, is powerful. However, you must judge by yourself whether the balanced position is valid. As the first route for a beginner, I think fixing first and checking one step at a time is suitable.
Limits of this continued analogy: The observed-variable model analyzes with positions fixed. But we can think that “the fixed points are actually wobbling a little, by the amount of measurement error” (this is dealt with under Question A in Section 4). The latent-variable model tries to handle even that wobble inside the model. That holds, however, only when the assumptions of the measurement model are satisfied. Nor does the analogy mean that “the observed-variable model is safe.” Even with fixed points only, when the springs increase, everything moves together, and other ways of connecting that fit equally well appear.


How the analogy maps onto the later discussion

“Interpretational confounding” corresponds to the placement of an invisible joint being changed by the pull of other springs.
“Checking measurement first (the two-step procedure)” corresponds to checking the invisible joint first, and handling it afterward.
The situations in which “there is a reason to consider a latent-variable model” correspond to situations where you want to handle even the wobble of the fixed points (measurement error) inside the model, or where you want to examine the relations among invisible joints themselves.




Examples of increased judgments
Here are four examples of judgments that increase. None of them is entirely absent from observed-variable models. But adding latent variables changes their weight greatly.
(1) Identification: This is the question of whether the number of unknowns in the model (the number of parameters to estimate) can be determined uniquely from the data. In a model where it cannot, the estimates are not determined. Observed-variable models also have identification problems, but with latent variables there are more points to decide, such as setting the unit of each latent variable.
(2) Balance between sample size and model complexity: In models with latent variables, the number of parameters to estimate often increases, so the balance between sample size and model complexity must be considered more carefully. The necessary sample size varies greatly with the number of factors, the number of indicators, the size of the factor loadings, the size of the path coefficients, the presence of missing data, the estimation method, and so on. A uniform rule of thumb is considered inappropriate. This article does not give numbers.
(3) How to read model fit: In models with latent variables, the match between the data and the model (model fit) is examined with several indices. Each index has its own meaning and limits, and there is no simple standard such as “this value is good.” There is also criticism of treating cutoff values as mechanical pass criteria.
(4) The relation between the measurement part and the structural part: In a typical latent-variable model, the measurement part and the structural part are in the end estimated within one model. As a result, the meaning of a latent variable is influenced not only by its own items but also by its relations with the other variables in the model. For example, when the specification of the structural part changes, the estimates of the measurement part (for example, factor loadings) also change, and the interpretation of what that latent variable substantively represents can change too. This is called the problem of “interpretational confounding.” Burt (1976) discussed, as this problem, that a latent variable can come to be given, in the course of estimation, a meaning different from the one the researcher gave it in advance.
There is also an idea of checking the measurement part first and then estimating the structural part (the two-step procedure). Anderson & Gerbing (1988) recommend first estimating and checking the measurement model, and take the position that being able to estimate in one step does not necessarily make it desirable. As a method that estimates the measurement part and the structural part separately, SAM (Rosseel & Loh, 2024) has been proposed. For SAM, the authors list as advantages that it is robust to local misspecification of the model, that convergence problems are less likely even with small samples, and that when the model is correctly specified the finite-sample bias is small. The authors position SAM as an estimation method, and distinguish it from the two-step procedure as a way of building a model. Let me state the difference in one sentence. In the procedure of regressing on mean scale scores, measurement error is not explicitly handled in the later model. SAM separates measurement and structure, but treats measurement error as a latent-variable model. They are similar in that “measurement comes first,” but they are not the same method. A latent-variable model does not necessarily “estimate everything at once.”
In an observed-variable model, building the scale (measurement) and running the regression or path analysis (structure) are done in separate stages. The results of each stage can be checked separately. I think this ease of separation is a great advantage for beginners.

title: Before adding latent variables: what scale building and path analysis can do
section: 4. When latent variables are needed and when they can be avoided
text:
4. When latent variables are needed and when they can be avoided
This section is the center of the article. It is also probably the part most open to debate. For that reason, I write the judgment in two stages.

Stage 1: Is there a need to use latent variables? Stage 2: Can the model be estimated and interpreted properly?

These are different questions. Stage 1 asks “is there a reason to use them?” and Stage 2 asks “are the conditions for using them in place?” For example, having a sufficient sample size is a Stage 2 condition. A sufficient sample size does not become a Stage 1 “reason to use.” Conversely, even if there is a reason at Stage 1, it is difficult to use the model if the Stage 2 conditions are not in place.

4.1 Stage 1: Is there a need to use latent variables?
First, let me describe a way of drawing the line that I think is not appropriate (this is only my opinion).
The division “use an observed-variable model when you want to know the size of associations between variables, and a latent-variable model when you want to know the structure among constructs” is often seen. But I think this division is not appropriate. This is because a regression or path analysis with subscale scores is also, in practice, examining associations among constructs. The type of research question alone cannot separate the two.
I place the dividing line not on the type of question but on how measurement is handled. Specifically, I judge from the following three questions.








Question
When I think an observed-variable model (that is, path analysis) is enough
When it is a reason to consider a latent-variable model




A. Do I need to estimate associations among constructs after explicitly modeling measurement error?
Reliability of the scales is sufficiently high, and I can judge that the effect of measurement error does not change the conclusion
The effect of measurement error could change the conclusion, and I want to take that effect into account explicitly


B. Is the measurement model itself the object of the research?
An existing scale or my own scale is used as a tool
I want to check the structure of the scale (the relation between items and constructs) as the center of the research


C. Do I need to verify that a scale has the same meaning across groups?
No group comparison; or equivalence is assumed, and I can state its basis and limits
Group comparison is central to the conclusion, and equivalence cannot be left as an assumption



This table is of course not a ranking of methods. It is for organizing the fit between a question and the conditions. Also, “an observed-variable model is enough” does not mean “a latent-variable model should be avoided.” It means “if you cannot explain the need, there is no hurry.”


4.2 Explaining each question of Stage 1
Question A: Is there a need to take measurement error into account explicitly?
In an observed-variable model, the subscale score is treated as a value without error. In fact, the score contains measurement error.
When there is measurement error, in a regression with one explanatory variable the coefficient tends to come out smaller than it should (this is called attenuation). When there are several explanatory variables and they are correlated, the situation is a little more complicated. The measurement error of one variable can bias the coefficients of other variables, and the direction of the bias can be either upward or downward. Rosseel & Loh (2024) also point out that measurement error remains in scale scores and factor scores, and that this can bias the regression coefficients in the structural part.
The size of this effect depends on the reliability of the scale. High reliability is a favorable condition for using an observed-variable model. But that alone does not let us judge that measurement error does not affect the conclusion, because the correlations among explanatory variables and other factors also bear on how large the effect on the coefficients is.
There is one thing I want to emphasize here. Low reliability is not solved by putting the scale into a latent-variable model. If reliability is low, the first thing to doubt is how the scale measures. You need to review the meaning of the items, the number of items, and how easy they are to answer. Putting a poor scale into a latent-variable model does not rescue it. However, reviewing the scale and the need to take measurement error into account are compatible. If, after improving the scale, the effect of measurement error could still change the conclusion, that is a reason to use latent variables.
A latent-variable model does not “remove” measurement error as if by magic. Under the assumptions of a specific measurement model, it models measurement error explicitly. So when the assumptions of the measurement model do not hold, the results also become difficult to interpret.
A high alpha is also not the whole of sufficient evidence for reliability. Alpha is one indicator of reliability, and it is also affected by the number of items and the nature of the items. The judgment should include, besides alpha, the content of the scale (the meaning of the items, stability over repeated measurement, and so on).
Question B: Is the measurement model itself the object of the research?
In a study that develops a new scale and puts the structure of measurement at the center of the paper, a model with latent variables (such as confirmatory factor analysis) is a natural choice. On the other hand, in a study that borrows an existing scale as a tool, verifying the structure of measurement is not the center of the research. In this case, I think it is reasonable to consider first the procedure of checking the scale and then building subscales.
Question C: Do I need to examine measurement invariance?
Suppose you want to check “whether a scale measures with the same meaning for men and women, or across countries.” To compare means across groups, the scale must have the same meaning across groups. This is called an examination of measurement invariance, and it is a representative analysis done with latent-variable models.
Simply comparing subscale scores cannot answer this question directly. However, there are methods related to measurement invariance outside SEM as well (item response theory, the examination of differential item functioning, and so on). Here I only say that the latent-variable model is a representative method.


4.3 Stage 2: Can the model be estimated and interpreted properly?
Suppose a reason to use latent variables was found at Stage 1. Next, at Stage 2, check the following points.







What to check
What to look at




Balance between sample size and model complexity
Is the sample size sufficient for the number of factors, indicators, and parameters? Do not rely on a uniform rule such as “at least N people.”


Identification
Is the model identified? Can you explain the identification conditions in your own words?


Estimation method and the nature of the data
How will you treat five-point scale data? Are the distributional assumptions reasonable?


Explaining the results
Can you explain the identification, the estimation method, and the judgment of model fit to readers and reviewers?



Whether data such as five-point scales can be treated as continuous is one of the points of debate. There are also estimation methods that treat them as ordered categories. However, depending on the number of categories and the shape of the distribution, methods that treat them as continuous may work well enough. It is not something to decide mechanically as “it is a five-point scale, so it must be an ordered-categorical method.”
I think the last row of this table, “can you explain it,” is the most important in practice. The results of research must be explainable to readers and reviewers. If you cannot answer questions such as “why did you include latent variables?”, “how did you check identification?”, and “how did you judge model fit?”, trust in the results is damaged.


4.4 Concrete examples
Example 1: A case where I think an observed-variable model is enough
Suppose a graduate student studies department-store customers, asking by questionnaire how “brand trust,” “perceived quality,” and “price acceptance” are associated with purchase intention. Existing scales are used, and each concept is measured with four or five items. The student has confirmed through factor analysis that there is no major problem in the structure of the items, and reliability is sufficient. No comparison between groups is made. Even if groups were compared, the student would not check that the scale has the same meaning across groups, but would place it as an assumption. In other words, the “checking whether the scale works in the same way across groups” in Question C of Stage 1 is not the purpose of this study. The sample size is small to medium.
In this case, I think it is reasonable to consider first the method of building subscales and running a regression analysis. This is because none of the three Stage 1 questions gives a strong reason to include latent variables. However, if it seems that the effect of measurement error could change the conclusion, I would review the decision at that point.
Example 2: A case where I think it is meaningful to consider a latent-variable model
A researcher wants to check whether a scale measures with the same meaning across countries, and then to compare the means across countries. The sample size in each country is also sufficient.
In this case, there is a clear reason under Question C of Stage 1. The Stage 2 conditions are also in place. The reason to use a latent-variable model is clear, and it can be explained.
The difference between the two examples is not the difficulty or the coolness of the method. It is whether the latent-variable model is needed for the question, and whether it can be handled properly.

title: Before adding latent variables: what scale building and path analysis can do
section: 5. How I recommend beginners proceed (my view)
text:
5. How I recommend beginners proceed (my view)
Let me summarize the discussion so far as advice for beginners.

First, build a scale and check it. Define the construct from theory, prepare the items, check them with factor analysis and alpha, and turn them into subscale scores. The details of this procedure are in the previous article.
Next, analyze with an observed-variable model. Use the subscales to run regression or path analysis. Because the results of each stage can be checked separately, this is a method in which mistakes are easy to notice and easy to explain. However, because subscale scores contain measurement error, the coefficients of the structural part can come out smaller than they should be, or biased (Question A in Section 4). Thinking about whether this effect could change the conclusion leads to the judgment in step 3.
Move to a latent-variable model once the need is visible. It is not too late to do so after a reason becomes clear in the research, such as wanting to take the effect of measurement error into account explicitly or wanting to check measurement invariance.

There is one thing I want to emphasize. “Being able to use a latent-variable model” and “being in a study that should use one” are different things.
There are also intermediate options between “estimate everything at once” and “do everything separately.” They are the two-step procedure that checks the measurement part first (Anderson & Gerbing, 1988) and methods that estimate measurement and structure separately (such as SAM; Rosseel & Loh, 2024).

title: Before adding latent variables: what scale building and path analysis can do
section: 6. Reference: for readers who want to know more
text:
6. Reference: for readers who want to know more
This section is a reference for readers who want to know more. It collects viewpoints for checking things by yourself before you use a latent-variable model.
The point of this section is not that “latent-variable models are bad.” It is that knowing what can happen when you use them without understanding their mathematical properties is useful.

6.1 Problems that can occur
(1) Good model fit does not mean the model is correct.
Model fit is an index of how well the data and the model match. There can be other models (equivalent models) that fit the same data equally well. MacCallum et al. (1993) examined 53 applied studies in psychology and showed that equivalent models often exist in large numbers. A good fit alone cannot show that “no other explanation holds.” I think we should not simply accept a statement like “the fit was good, so the hypothesis was supported.”
(2) The identification problem
In a model that is not identified, the estimates are not determined uniquely. Software may still output numbers. But it may be impossible to explain what those numbers mean.
(3) Interpretational confounding
As touched on in Section 3, depending on the specification of the structural part, the estimates of the measurement part (factor loadings and so on) are affected, and the interpretation of what a latent variable substantively represents may change (Burt, 1976). Burt states that when the covariances among the items of a latent variable are low, and the covariances between those items and the items of other latent variables differ widely, the meaning of that latent variable in simultaneous estimation is easily swayed by variation in the items of the other latent variables (he cites an earlier analysis of latent variables with two indicators). For this reason, I think scales whose items are only weakly related need more attention. It is good to keep this point in mind in your own analyses as well.
(4) Trial and error with modification indices
When the fit is poor, you can revise the model following the “modification indices” that software shows (quite a few people accept these modifications uncritically). However, if you keep revising the model by looking at the data, you end up fitting the model to chance features specific to that data. It is worth checking whether you record and report why and in what order you revised the model.
(5) Assumptions of estimation
Standard estimation methods place certain assumptions on the distribution of the data. As touched on in Section 4, how to treat data such as five-point scales is one of the points of debate. When the sample size is small relative to the model, estimation may go badly, or improper solutions (such as negative variances) may appear.
(6) Reading causation into the results
When you draw arrows in a path analysis or a latent-variable model, it is easy for readers to take them as showing causal relations. In cross-sectional surveys, arrows represent the researcher’s assumptions and are not proof of causation. In reports, I think it is safer to write “association.”
(7) Problems in choosing a method
If you cannot reproduce the results by yourself, or cannot explain them, it becomes difficult to notice mistakes and difficult to have others check them. In an observed-variable model, measurement and structure can be checked stage by stage, and it is easier to trace at which stage the results changed. In a latent-variable model, many parameters move together, so isolating where a problem lies requires more understanding.


6.2 A checklist of questions for choosing a method
I have put the questions to ask yourself when choosing a method into a checklist.
Before using a latent-variable model, please ask yourself the following.

Can I explain in one sentence why I include latent variables? (Which of the Stage 1 questions applies?)
What is missing from subscales and an observed-variable model?
Can I explain my choices of sample size, identification, and estimation method in my own words? (Stage 2)
If I revised the model with modification indices, do I have a record of it?
Even when the fit is good, did I consider other explanations?
Is the way I write the results a causal claim?



6.3 In fairness
Latent-variable models are of course wonderful methods. They are used for estimating associations with measurement error explicitly taken into account, for verifying measurement invariance, and for studies that take measurement itself as the subject. In such studies, a latent-variable model is an excellent tool. If you can use it properly, you should use it actively.
It is not about giving up on using them. What matters is to check whether your reason for using them is rooted in the research question, and whether you can explain the results in your own words. That is what I think.

title: Before adding latent variables: what scale building and path analysis can do
text:
Closing
To repeat, a latent-variable model is a powerful tool. Because it is powerful, I think it is good to use it in a state in which you can explain why you use it.
For beginners, I recommend the path of building and checking a scale and then analyzing with an observed-variable model. As you accumulate that experience, the situations in which a latent-variable model becomes necessary, such as “here I want to take measurement error into account explicitly” and “here I want to examine measurement itself,” will come into view naturally. That is the next step.

title: Paper Guide: Quantitative and Qualitative Research Are Two Cultures, Not Rivals (Mahoney & Goertz, 2006)
text:
Reference: Mahoney, J., & Goertz, G. (2006). A tale of two cultures: Contrasting quantitative and qualitative research. Political Analysis, 14(3), 227-249. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpj017
Summary: This paper organizes quantitative and qualitative research not as a contest between better and worse, but as two cultures with different goals. I recommend it as required reading for anyone designing a research project. The paper shows that deciding first which kind of question you are asking makes it easier to choose an analytical method.

title: Paper Guide: Quantitative and Qualitative Research Are Two Cultures, Not Rivals (Mahoney & Goertz, 2006)
text:
Overview
Quantitative research, which is built on statistics and aims to learn “average effects,” and qualitative research (case study research), which aims to pin down “the cause of a particular event,” ask different questions in the first place. Relatively speaking, quantitative research asks how much a cause affects outcomes on average, whereas qualitative research asks why this outcome happened in this case. The paper shows that the practices of both traditions are reasonable given their respective goals.

title: Paper Guide: Quantitative and Qualitative Research Are Two Cultures, Not Rivals (Mahoney & Goertz, 2006)
text:
Why I chose this paper
In MBA research and business research, you may run into this wall: A/B tests and regression analysis reveal the overall trend, yet you still cannot tell why your single most important customer left.
This paper offers a way to think about why that happens. Measuring the “average trend” across the data and tracing the “causal mechanism” of an individual event are two different ways of thinking. The paper can be read as a “map of thinking” for choosing an analytical method that fits the question you want to answer. I chose it because I believe it is one of the papers MBA students should read before starting their own research.

title: Paper Guide: Quantitative and Qualitative Research Are Two Cultures, Not Rivals (Mahoney & Goertz, 2006)
text:
The structure of the paper
The paper contrasts the two traditions across 10 areas (approaches to explanation, conceptions of causation, multivariate explanations, equifinality, scope and causal generalization, case selection practices, weighting observations, substantively important cases, lack of fit, and concepts and measurement). In this memo, to make the overall picture easier to grasp, I narrow them down to three: the purpose of the question, how causation is understood, and how cases are selected. For the other areas, please check the paper itself.








Three axes
Qualitative culture (the detective’s view)
Quantitative culture (the experimenter’s view)




Purpose of the question
Explain why the outcome happened in a particular case
Measure how much a factor affects outcomes on average


How causation is understood
Thinks in terms of the “multiplication” (combination) of conditions
Typically thinks in terms of the “addition” (average effects) of variables


How cases are selected
Examines in depth mainly the cases in which the outcome occurred
To avoid bias, does not select cases on the outcome (the dependent variable)



Reading the table from left to right, you can see that the differences between the two cultures are connected in a single line. The paper likens qualitative research to a detective. Quantitative research, by contrast, is explained as statistical methods that take the logic of the controlled experiment as their model. The phrase “the experimenter’s view” in this article is simply a label I use for this contrast.
A detective wants to know the cause of a crime that has already happened, so the detective examines in depth the cases in which it happened. The detective also assumes that the cause is not one thing but a combination of several conditions.
An experimenter, on the other hand, wants to know the average effect of a factor, and therefore takes care not to select cases by their outcome, which would introduce bias. The experimenter also thinks of the effects of the factors as adding up.
If the goals differ, then both how cases are selected and how causation is understood differ as well.

title: Paper Guide: Quantitative and Qualitative Research Are Two Cultures, Not Rivals (Mahoney & Goertz, 2006)
text:
The paper’s contributions
First, the paper makes the difference in the “goal of the question” clearly visible. The question “why did this case happen?” and the question “what effect does this factor have on average?” are different questions. Much of the reason why debates about analytical methods fail to connect lies not in which method is better, but in this difference in purpose.
Second, the paper shines a light on “combinations of conditions.” A factor may not work on its own; sometimes an outcome appears only “when conditions A, B, and C are all present.” Moreover, there may be more than one route to the same outcome (this is called equifinality). The paper organizes, in a logical way, this feature of the real world that is easy to overlook in models that simply add effects together.

From here on, these are my own views, based on the paper.

title: Paper Guide: Quantitative and Qualitative Research Are Two Cultures, Not Rivals (Mahoney & Goertz, 2006)
text:
What I found noteworthy
What I consider especially important about this paper is that it lets us understand qualitative and quantitative research by contrasting them. Seeing the two side by side makes clear what each aims for and why each works the way it does.
Another point is that it can serve as a foundation for understanding QCA as a method. If you grasp the logic of qualitative research (combinations of conditions, multiple routes), you can see what QCA has inherited.

title: Paper Guide: Quantitative and Qualitative Research Are Two Cultures, Not Rivals (Mahoney & Goertz, 2006)
section: Thinking about business applications: the case of customer churn
text:
Thinking about business applications: the case of customer churn
Let us step away from the paper and think about applications. Consider an e-commerce company analyzing customer churn (the numbers are a made-up example to aid understanding).
Quantitative approaches such as statistics and A/B tests are well suited to revealing the overall trend, for example “issuing a coupon lowers the churn rate across all customers by 3% on average.” However, this alone does not reveal the individual reason why Customer A, who had spent the most with the company, suddenly stopped using the service.
This is where a qualitative, logic-based approach comes in. It can bring out candidate combinations: churn tends to occur when several conditions overlap, such as “a delivery delay,” “dissatisfaction with the support response,” and “a competitor’s discount campaign.” However, this does not establish the cause; it is material for hypotheses to be checked later.

title: Paper Guide: Quantitative and Qualitative Research Are Two Cultures, Not Rivals (Mahoney & Goertz, 2006)
text:
Connection to QCA
This paper organized the differences between the qualitative and quantitative cultures. One method that connects the two is QCA (qualitative comparative analysis). It keeps the qualitative way of thinking, which emphasizes combinations of conditions and multiple routes, while analyzing a dataset systematically. I also discuss the ideas behind QCA in the article Why QCA suits decision-making on this blog.

Summary points for review

title: Paper Guide: Quantitative and Qualitative Research Are Two Cultures, Not Rivals (Mahoney & Goertz, 2006)
text:
Points to revisit

Before starting an analysis, decide whether your question is “why did this case happen?” or “how does this factor work on average?”
Once the question is decided, how to select cases and how to understand causation follow naturally.
When you study QCA, return to this paper’s ideas of “combinations of conditions” and “multiple routes.”

title: Paper Guide: Quantitative and Qualitative Research Are Two Cultures, Not Rivals (Mahoney & Goertz, 2006)
text:
Glossary

Causes-of-effects: A detective-style question that works backward from an outcome: “Why did this happen?”
Effects-of-causes: An experimenter-style question that measures the average effect of adding a factor: “What effect does this factor have on average?”
Equifinality: The fact that there is not just one route to the same outcome, but several.

title: QCA in marketing and management: ten papers to read first (applications)
text:
The basics list introduced the standard readings for learning QCA. The next question is probably “How is it actually used in research?” Here are papers from marketing and management that are worth reading as models for your own work, together with the theoretical background from management and organization research, grouped by purpose.
As in the basics list, the summaries stay within what the publishers’ abstracts say.

title: QCA in marketing and management: ten papers to read first (applications)
text:
1. Applications in marketing and services

Ordanini, A., Parasuraman, A., & Rubera, G. (2014). When the recipe is more important than the ingredients: A qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) of service innovation configurations. Journal of Service Research, 17(2), 134-149. https://doi.org/10.1177/1094670513513337 Studies luxury hotel services and uses QCA to examine which combinations of attributes lead to the adoption of a new service. An application that looks not only at individual attributes but at how they are combined.
Frambach, R. T., Fiss, P. C., & Ingenbleek, P. T. M. (2016). How important is customer orientation for firm performance? A fuzzy set analysis of orientations, strategies, and environments. Journal of Business Research, 69(4), 1428-1436. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbusres.2015.10.120 Combines customer orientation with other strategic orientations, strategy types, and market environments, and uses fsQCA to find the configurations that go with high firm performance. An application that considers the role of customer orientation through its combinations with other conditions.

title: QCA in marketing and management: ten papers to read first (applications)
section: 2. Theoretical background in management and organization research
text:
2. Theoretical background in management and organization research

Fiss, P. C. (2007). A set-theoretic approach to organizational configurations. Academy of Management Review, 32(4), 1180-1198. https://doi.org/10.5465/amr.2007.26586092 Treats an organization as a combination of elements and argues for analyzing the link between those combinations and outcomes with set theory. A foundation for thinking about several combinations that lead to the same outcome.
Fiss, P. C. (2011). Building better causal theories: A fuzzy set approach to typologies in organization research. Academy of Management Journal, 54(2), 393-420. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2011.60263120 Analyzes organizational typologies with fuzzy sets and examines the combinations of conditions that lead to an outcome. Important for understanding that the causes can be asymmetric between the presence and the absence of an outcome.
Woodside, A. G. (2013). Moving beyond multiple regression analysis to algorithms: Calling for adoption of a paradigm shift from symmetric to asymmetric thinking in data analysis and crafting theory. Journal of Business Research, 66(4), 463-472. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbusres.2012.12.021 Alongside the effects of single variables in multiple regression, it proposes an analysis that looks at combinations of conditions and at causal asymmetry. It discusses how to analyze data and build theory, using regression and fsQCA on the same data.
Misangyi, V. F., Greckhamer, T., Furnari, S., Fiss, P. C., Crilly, D., & Aguilera, R. (2017). Embracing causal complexity: The emergence of a neo-configurational perspective. Journal of Management, 43(1), 255-282. https://doi.org/10.1177/0149206316679252 Reviews how QCA has developed in management and organization research and sets out a “neo-configurational perspective” for capturing causal complexity. It links set membership, necessity and sufficiency, and counterfactual analysis to theoretical viewpoints.

title: QCA in marketing and management: ten papers to read first (applications)
section: 3. How to run and report an analysis (practical guides)
text:
3. How to run and report an analysis (practical guides)

Greckhamer, T., Furnari, S., Fiss, P. C., & Aguilera, R. V. (2018). Studying configurations with qualitative comparative analysis: Best practices in strategy and organization research. Strategic Organization, 16(4), 482-495. https://doi.org/10.1177/1476127018786487 Sets out practical guidelines for QCA in strategy and organization research. It covers the whole course of a study, from model building and case selection to calibration, analysis, reporting, and interpretation.
Pappas, I. O., & Woodside, A. G. (2021). Fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA): Guidelines for research practice in information systems and marketing. International Journal of Information Management, 58, Article 102310. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijinfomgt.2021.102310 A practical guide to using fsQCA in information systems and marketing research. It explains the procedure with data from earlier studies and also touches on checking predictive validity and combining fsQCA with methods such as SEM.
Park, Y., Fiss, P. C., & El Sawy, O. A. (2020). Theorizing the multiplicity of digital phenomena: The ecology of configurations, causal recipes, and guidelines for applying QCA. MIS Quarterly, 44(4), 1493-1520. https://doi.org/10.25300/MISQ/2020/13879 For digital phenomena that involve several theoretical perspectives and combinations of conditions, it offers a framework that ties QCA to theory building. Through examples, it explains how to apply QCA to deductive theory testing and to inductive theory building.

title: QCA in marketing and management: ten papers to read first (applications)
text:
4. Choosing the threshold

Krogslund, C., Choi, D. D., & Poertner, M. (2015). Fuzzy sets on shaky ground: Parameter sensitivity and confirmation bias in fsQCA. Political Analysis, 23(1), 21-41. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpu016 Argues that fsQCA results can change with small changes in the parameters a user chooses, and that combinations containing randomly generated variables are often found to be sufficient for an outcome. It re-analyzes three existing studies and uses sensitivity analyses and Monte Carlo simulations.

On how the placement of the threshold changes the results, see also Toyoda (2026), Quality & Quantity, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11135-026-03092-3.

title: From survey items to a scale, then on to regression and QCA: a step-by-step guide
text:
NoteHow this article, the app, and the R script fit together



The step-by-step articles on this blog come with an app (a tool that runs in your browser) that lets you try the same procedure. The three have different roles:

The article explains the ideas and the procedure. The calculations are shown as R code.
The app (Scale Maker) reads your data (CSV) and shows the same calculations as the article on screen. You can learn the flow of the procedure and the meaning of the numbers without using R.
The R script: the app can produce an R script that reproduces the results of your settings on screen. You can run it in R and confirm that the numbers match the app. In research, you can also keep the script as a record of your analysis.

If you use R, start from the code in the article. If you learn with the app, read the article while looking at the numbers in the app first, and then reproduce them with the R script when you are comfortable.

title: From survey items to a scale, then on to regression and QCA: a step-by-step guide
text:
The question this article answers
Research in marketing and management deals with concepts such as brand trust, perceived quality, customer satisfaction, and price sensitivity, which are hard to measure with a single question. These concepts are called constructs, and we measure them with several questionnaire items.
Suppose we measure brand trust with these three items:

Q1: This brand is sincere
Q2: I think this brand keeps its promises
Q3: I feel secure using this brand

What we want to know is not the effect of Q1, Q2, or Q3 separately. We want to know how brand trust, the three items taken together, relates to outcomes such as purchase intention. We also often want to use such constructs in later analyses: regression, logistic regression, QCA, cluster analysis, decision trees, and so on.
Structural equation modeling (SEM) is a wonderful method, but you do not have to start with it (and if you use it without understanding its characteristics, it can do more harm than good). What matters is not which method is more advanced, but how you measure the constructs of your research, and how you analyze them in the way that best fits your research question.
This article presents a procedure that works well for MBA research and empirical studies, with an example in R. The example data are generated with random numbers (they are not real survey data).

Scope of this article

We deal with constructs that you define in advance from theory and measure with several items. This does not deny the value of exploratory studies that look for constructs in the data.
We deal with measurement like brand trust, where we assume that one underlying construct drives the answers to several items in common. A person with high brand trust answers high on Q1, Q2, and Q3 alike. Therefore, the items are expected to correlate with one another (this kind of measurement is called reflective measurement).
A different case is building a “customer behavior index” by combining purchase frequency, purchase amount, and years of use. A person who buys often does not necessarily spend a lot. The items need not correlate strongly, so the factor analysis and alpha procedure shown here does not apply as it is. It is not true that “for any index, you can raise alpha and take the average.”

title: From survey items to a scale, then on to regression and QCA: a step-by-step guide
text:
The overall flow

Define the construct from theory and prior research
Prepare several questionnaire items for each construct
Use exploratory factor analysis (EFA) to examine, in an exploratory way, whether the item groupings you expected are consistent with the data
Align the direction of reverse-keyed items
Check internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha)
Build subscales by averaging items
Use the subscales in regression and QCA

Let us go through them in order.






TipFor readers who learn with the app (this article)



“Example 3” in the app (Scale Maker) uses the same data as this article. Steps 2 to 7 in the app correspond to steps 3 to 6 in this article. Regression and QCA are done in R. The app’s calculation is the same as R’s standard promax. Depending on the version of psych, the third decimal place of the factor loadings can differ slightly.

title: From survey items to a scale, then on to regression and QCA: a step-by-step guide
section: Step 1: Define the construct from theory (before factor analysis)
text:
Step 1: Define the construct from theory (before factor analysis)
This is the most important step. Before factor analysis, the researcher has to decide what to measure. Concepts such as “brand trust” and “perceived quality” are not things that statistical software finds for you automatically.
The approach to avoid looks like this:

“Let’s ask 20 questions for now, run a factor analysis, and name the factors that come out.”

This is a misunderstanding that beginners especially tend to fall into. The preferred order is as follows.
From prior research and theory, define what brand trust is, and think about the questionnaire items needed to observe it. When you prepared Q1 to Q3 above, you already held a theoretical expectation before the survey began: “these three items should be measuring one construct, brand trust.” You then run a factor analysis to check whether these three items actually move in the same direction in the real response data.
\[
\text{theory} \rightarrow \text{construct definition} \rightarrow \text{item design} \rightarrow \text{data collection} \rightarrow \text{consistency check by factor analysis}
\]
We do not build theory from factor analysis; we examine, in an exploratory way, whether the data are consistent with a measurement structure that we assumed from theory. This is why research on prior studies and theory beforehand is so important.

Factor analysis is not a machine that sorts items automatically
Suppose you run a factor analysis on 20 items and get four factors. That alone does not let you say that “human attitudes consist of four constructs.” What factor analysis shows is only the statistical fact that “in this sample, the correlation structure of this item set can be summarized fairly well by about four common factors.”
Whether those four factors are brand trust, quality evaluation, or brand attachment is not decided by the statistical result. You have to interpret them using prior research, the content of the items, the definition of the construct, and the purpose of the research. Please avoid giving plausible-sounding names to whatever factors come out.


Statistical grouping and theoretical validity are different things
Suppose four items, “high quality,” “good design,” “reasonably priced,” and “a well-known brand,” group into one factor statistically. That alone does not mean you may call the factor “brand value.” There are several possible reasons why items group statistically:

They really measure the same construct
Respondents tend to rate everything high
There is a halo effect
The item wordings are similar
There is a method effect from the same response format

A high factor loading does not prove that the items belong to the same concept in theory.

title: From survey items to a scale, then on to regression and QCA: a step-by-step guide
section: Step 2: Prepare several items for each construct
text:
Step 2: Prepare several items for each construct
As a rule, prepare several items for each construct. Do not line up items that merely rephrase the same sentence. Items with the same meaning tend to raise Cronbach’s alpha, but this does not mean that the construct is covered adequately. It is desirable for the items to represent different aspects of the construct appropriately.
For example, compare these two ways of measuring brand trust.
An example of rephrasing

This brand is trustworthy
This brand is reliable
This brand is dependable

All three ask almost the same thing. The answers will be similar, so alpha will be high. But if you duplicate content to raise alpha, you can no longer tell whether the necessary aspects of brand trust are covered. Whether they are covered has to be examined separately. Note that when the concept you want to measure is narrow, items with close meanings can be appropriate, and they can also help average out errors caused by differences in wording.
An example of different aspects

I think this brand keeps its promises (the aspect of fulfilling promises)
This brand is sincere (the aspect of caring about the other party)
I feel secure using this brand (the aspect of reassurance in use)

All three are part of “brand trust,” but each looks at a different aspect, so the concept is captured more broadly. However, if you vary the aspects too much, the correlations among items fall and the items no longer form one factor. In light of the definition of the construct, choose items within the range where you can say they are “different aspects of the same concept.”






TipA questionnaire tip: labeling the options of a 7-point scale



There are two main ways to label the options.

Put a verbal label on all seven options: the meaning of each option is clear. On the other hand, words such as “very,” “extremely,” and “quite” feel different in strength to different people.
Label only the two ends and leave only numbers in between: this makes it easier to avoid differences in how strongly the words are felt.

Disagree  1 - 2 - 3 - 4 - 5 - 6 - 7  Agree
Which one to use depends on the purpose of the research and on the format of the existing scale you use. What deserves attention is that, in either form, treating the scores as equally spaced numbers is the analyst’s assumption (a simplification). The way of labeling does not guarantee equal spacing. In this article, we treat responses as numbers under this assumption.


If a scale has been used widely in prior research, using the existing scale is often better than writing items from scratch, because its validity has been examined and it is easy to compare with other studies. This does not mean, however, that “the existing study used three items, so we can use them as they are.” If the industry, culture, respondents, or purpose of the survey differ, the same factor structure may not be reproduced. Even with an existing scale, it is worth checking the structure in your own data.

title: From survey items to a scale, then on to regression and QCA: a step-by-step guide
text:
Example data
From here we follow the steps in R. Suppose we measured nine items on a 7-point scale. The theoretical expectation is the following three constructs.



Construct
Item
Wording (example)




Brand trust
Q1
This brand is sincere



Q2
I think this brand keeps its promises



Q3
I feel secure using this brand


Perceived quality
Q4
This brand’s products are of high quality



Q5
This brand’s products perform well



Q6 (reverse-keyed)
The quality of this brand’s products varies


Price sensitivity
Q7
I notice even small price differences



Q8
I am tempted to buy when there is a discount



Q9
If products are similar, I choose the cheaper one



The wordings are examples (the data are generated with random numbers, and no actual survey corresponds to these wordings).
The outcome variable Y is purchase intention (one item on a 7-point scale).






Note



In this article, we treat 7-point responses as numbers and use Pearson correlation and linear regression. This is a common simplification in practice. If the response distributions are strongly skewed, you can also consider treating them as ordinal. For example, in factor analysis you can use polychoric correlations (fa(..., cor = "poly")). If purchase intention is measured with a single item, you can choose ordinal logistic regression instead of linear regression.


The following code creates the example data (the random seed is fixed, so you get the same data).

set.seed(2026)
n   <- 300
Phi <- matrix(c(1.0, 0.5, -0.2,
                0.5, 1.0, -0.1,
               -0.2,-0.1,  1.0), 3, 3, byrow = TRUE)   # correlations among the 3 constructs
Fm  <- matrix(rnorm(n * 3), n) %*% chol(Phi)
lam <- c(.80,.75,.70,  .78,.72,.68,  .75,.70,.65)       # item loadings (the "true" values)
fac <- rep(1:3, each = 3)
to7 <- function(z) as.integer(cut(z, c(-Inf,-1.6,-1.0,-0.4,0.4,1.0,1.6,Inf)))  # make 7-point responses
X <- sapply(1:9, function(j) to7(lam[j] * Fm[, fac[j]] + sqrt(1 - lam[j]^2) * rnorm(n)))
X[, 6] <- 8L - X[, 6]                                    # record Q6 as a reverse-keyed item
colnames(X) <- paste0("Q", 1:9)
b <- c(.45, .30, -.20)                       # effects of the 3 constructs on purchase intention
v <- drop(t(b) %*% Phi %*% b)                # variance of the signal part (including correlations among the constructs)
Y <- to7(drop(Fm %*% b) + sqrt(1 - v) * rnorm(n))   # add error so that the total variance is 1
dat <- data.frame(X, Y = Y)
head(dat)

  Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4 Q5 Q6 Q7 Q8 Q9 Y
1  5  5  3  3  3  3  4  4  6 6
2  2  4  2  3  3  5  5  4  5 3
3  4  4  3  3  4  5  5  6  3 4
4  5  4  4  4  5  1  5  4  4 3
5  4  4  4  4  2  7  3  4  4 4
6  2  1  1  2  2  6  4  5  5 1

title: From survey items to a scale, then on to regression and QCA: a step-by-step guide
section: Step 3: Examine how the items group, with exploratory factor analysis
text:
Step 3: Examine how the items group, with exploratory factor analysis
Once the items are ready, examine how they group by using exploratory factor analysis (EFA). The role we expect of EFA here is not “to invent constructs from a state of knowing nothing.” It is to examine, in an exploratory way, whether the item structure we assumed from theory is consistent with the actual data. EFA is different from confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), which specifies in advance as a model which item measures which factor and tests it. The result of EFA is material for judging consistency with your expectation; it does not mean that the measurement structure has been verified.
First, as a guide to the number of factors, look at the eigenvalues of the correlation matrix and at parallel analysis. The count of eigenvalues of 1 or more is only a rough guide. Parallel analysis compares the eigenvalues of the real data with those obtained from random data, and uses the comparison as a clue to the number of factors. Decide the number of factors together with your theoretical expectation. Then extract three factors by principal axis factoring with promax rotation.

library(psych)
items <- paste0("Q", 1:9)
round(eigen(cor(dat[, items]))$values, 3)

[1] 2.918 1.921 1.107 0.640 0.584 0.528 0.490 0.462 0.350

set.seed(2026)
fa.parallel(dat[, items], fa = "fa", fm = "pa")   # parallel analysis (a figure appears)








Parallel analysis suggests that the number of factors =  3  and the number of components =  NA 

fa3 <- fa(dat[, items], nfactors = 3, fm = "pa", rotate = "Promax",
          min.err = 1e-8, max.iter = 1000)   # strict convergence criteria for the iterations

Loading required namespace: GPArotation

print(fa3$loadings, cutoff = 0.3)


Loadings:
   PA1    PA3    PA2   
Q1         0.731       
Q2         0.724       
Q3         0.582       
Q4  0.769              
Q5  0.775              
Q6 -0.632              
Q7                0.695
Q8                0.674
Q9                0.639

                PA1   PA3   PA2
SS loadings    1.62 1.430 1.350
Proportion Var 0.18 0.159 0.150
Cumulative Var 0.18 0.339 0.489

round(fa3$Phi, 2)

     PA1   PA3   PA2
PA1 1.00  0.54  0.01
PA3 0.54  1.00 -0.20
PA2 0.01 -0.20  1.00








Note



To make the results easy to reproduce, this article uses rotate = "Promax" (with a capital P). The lowercase "promax" is not wrong, but its internal normalization differs, so the values change slightly.
min.err = 1e-8, max.iter = 1000 makes the iterations of principal axis factoring converge under strict criteria. The default criteria are loose, so the extraction can differ slightly around the third decimal place. To make the results match, this article uses the strict criteria.
Note also that the promax rotation calculation differs a little between versions of psych, and the third decimal place of the loadings can change (we confirmed a difference of at most 0.003 between psych 2.4.1 and 2.6.5). The extraction (principal axis factoring) gives the same result. The interpretation does not change.


Here is what to look at.

Number of factors: Look at the eigenvalues (the number of those at 1 or more) and the parallel analysis figure (the number of factors whose real-data eigenvalues exceed those from random data), and check whether they are consistent with the three factors we expected from theory.
Item groupings: Check whether Q1 to Q3, Q4 to Q6, and Q7 to Q9 load on the same factor, as expected. (Labels such as PA1 only indicate the order. Read the meaning of a factor from the items that load on it.)
The negative loading of Q6: Q6 has the opposite sign to Q4 and Q5 within the same factor. This is a clue that Q6 may be a reverse-keyed item. However, the sign is only a guide (the sign of a whole factor can be flipped). Whether an item is reverse-keyed is decided by the meaning of the wording.
Whether any item loads strongly on several factors (cross-loading).

For example, if only Q3 loaded strongly on the perceived quality factor, consider the following before deleting it:

Was the wording of Q3 appropriate?
Are brand trust and perceived quality conceptually too close?
Is there a problem with the translation or the phrasing?
Did respondents read it with a meaning different from the one we expected?

Use the result of EFA not as a “keep or delete verdict,” but as material for understanding the gap between the measurement model assumed from theory and the actual response behavior. If you mechanically delete a content-wise important item only because its loading is a little low, you may damage content validity.

title: From survey items to a scale, then on to regression and QCA: a step-by-step guide
section: Step 4: Align the direction of reverse-keyed items
text:
Step 4: Align the direction of reverse-keyed items
Q6 is a reverse-keyed item. In practice, it is easier to follow if you decide the reverse-keyed items from the meaning of the wording before the analysis and align their direction in advance. In this article, we ran the EFA first, to show that a negative loading can be a clue. Use the minimum and maximum of the scale (here 1 and 7) and compute (minimum + maximum) − original value, that is, 8 - Q6. For 1 to 7, use 8 - Q6; for 1 to 5, use 6 - Q6. The same formula also works for a scale whose minimum is not 1 (for example, 0 to 10). Use the ends of the scale on the questionnaire (1 and 7 for a 7-point scale), not the minimum and maximum observed in the data. Whether an item is reverse-keyed is decided by the meaning of the wording (theory).

dat$Q6r <- 8 - dat$Q6

title: From survey items to a scale, then on to regression and QCA: a step-by-step guide
text:
Step 5: Check internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha)
Once you have examined the factor structure, check the internal consistency of each item group. A typical index is Cronbach’s alpha. For example, \(\alpha = .84\) indicates that the item group has relatively high internal consistency.

a_trust   <- alpha(dat[, c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3")],  check.keys = FALSE)
a_quality <- alpha(dat[, c("Q4", "Q5", "Q6r")], check.keys = FALSE)
a_price   <- alpha(dat[, c("Q7", "Q8", "Q9")],  check.keys = FALSE)
round(c(trust   = a_trust$total$raw_alpha,
        quality = a_quality$total$raw_alpha,
        price   = a_price$total$raw_alpha), 3)

  trust quality   price 
  0.731   0.774   0.705 


There are two points to note.

A high alpha does not prove a one-factor structure. Alpha is an index of internal consistency, not an index for verifying factor structure. Also, alpha alone cannot tell you about reliability in general or about validity. The order is: examine the structure by factor analysis, then check the internal consistency of that item group.
Alpha tends to rise as the number of items grows. If needed, you may use McDonald’s omega alongside it.

title: From survey items to a scale, then on to regression and QCA: a step-by-step guide
text:
Step 6: Build the subscales
Once you have examined the structure and checked the internal consistency, build a subscale for each construct. Usually the simple mean of the items is the default.
\[
\text{Trust} = \frac{Q_1 + Q_2 + Q_3}{3}, \qquad
\text{Quality} = \frac{Q_4 + Q_5 + Q_{6r}}{3}
\]

dat$Trust   <- rowMeans(dat[, c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3")])
dat$Quality <- rowMeans(dat[, c("Q4", "Q5", "Q6r")])
dat$Price   <- rowMeans(dat[, c("Q7", "Q8", "Q9")])
round(cor(dat[, c("Trust", "Quality", "Price")]), 2)

        Trust Quality Price
Trust    1.00    0.43 -0.14
Quality  0.43    1.00  0.01
Price   -0.14    0.01  1.00


A scale built from a simple mean still contains measurement error. An ordinary regression that uses such a scale does not model the measurement error explicitly. Therefore, the coefficients you obtain are not necessarily the same as the relationships among the latent constructs themselves. With low reliability, this effect can be larger. In multiple regression especially, the effect of measurement error also depends on the correlations among the predictors, so you cannot judge the effect on the coefficients from reliability alone.
A simple mean has the following advantages:

The calculation is clear and highly reproducible
It depends relatively little on the sample
The unit of the original response scale is kept, so it is easy to interpret
It can be used in both regression and QCA


Why not use factor scores?
Using factor scores is not wrong in itself. However, factor scores have problems: the weights depend on the sample, the values change with the estimation method, the meaning of the score itself is hard to grasp, and the scale may not be the same in another sample. Unless there is a special reason, a policy of using simple-mean scales whose reliability has been checked is quite reasonable for MBA-level research.


Where does confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) come in?
In exploratory MBA research, it is practical to build simple-mean scales based on the content of the items, the EFA results, and internal consistency. However, that alone does not mean that the validity of the measurement has been fully established.
How far to verify depends on the track record of verification of an existing scale, the extent of your changes, and the strength of the claim the research needs to make. When you want to verify the measurement structure explicitly, or when you have built a new scale or changed one substantially, consider additional verification such as CFA. In CFA, you specify in advance, as a model, which item measures which factor. If an existing measurement model is clear, you can also start with CFA without going through EFA. So there is no fixed order of “always do CFA after EFA.”
If your sample is large enough, a better approach is to split the sample, running EFA on one part for exploration and CFA on the other for verification. Even if you do run CFA, you do not necessarily have to use the CFA factor scores afterward.

title: From survey items to a scale, then on to regression and QCA: a step-by-step guide
section: Step 7: Use the subscales in regression and QCA
text:
Step 7: Use the subscales in regression and QCA

Regression
Once you have the subscales, you can run an ordinary regression.
\[
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Trust} + \beta_2 \text{Quality} + \beta_3 \text{Price} + \varepsilon
\]

summary(lm(Y ~ Trust + Quality + Price, data = dat))


Call:
lm(formula = Y ~ Trust + Quality + Price, data = dat)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-3.11817 -0.87767  0.06223  0.76259  2.85718 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  1.42862    0.37338   3.826 0.000159 ***
Trust        0.57160    0.06622   8.632 3.78e-16 ***
Quality      0.36507    0.05991   6.093 3.44e-09 ***
Price       -0.27133    0.05812  -4.668 4.61e-06 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 1.157 on 296 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.4399,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.4342 
F-statistic: 77.49 on 3 and 296 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16




QCA
QCA needs a value of each condition for each case. In this example, the subscales of brand trust, perceived quality, and price sensitivity can be used as conditions. In fuzzy-set QCA (fsQCA), you calibrate each of them into set membership (values from 0 to 1). The outcome, purchase intention Y, is also calibrated into the set “high purchase intention.”
Then, for example, for the combination “high brand trust, high perceived quality, and low price sensitivity,” we examine a sufficiency relation such as the following (~ is negation and * is logical AND).
\[
\mathrm{TRUST} * \mathrm{QUALITY} * {\sim}\mathrm{PRICE} \rightarrow \mathrm{PURCHASE}
\]
Points to note:

This expression is not an analysis result. It is an example of a combination to examine.
Decide the calibration anchors (full membership, full non-membership, and the crossover point) from the meaning of the set, not by mechanically converting the scale mean to a 0 to 1 range.
Y in the example measures purchase “intention.” Please write it separately from actual purchase “behavior.”

For the calibration and the analysis in practice, see the ThSQCA for beginners series.


What it means to use regression and QCA together
If you run regression and QCA on the same subscales, you can look at the same phenomenon from different viewpoints. Regression looks at the average association when the other variables are held constant. QCA looks at which combinations of conditions lead to the outcome. The two are better seen as complementary methods with different viewpoints than as competing methods. If you use common subscales, the measurement is unified across the two analyses.

title: From survey items to a scale, then on to regression and QCA: a step-by-step guide
text:
What to report
In a paper or report, writing at least the following lets readers follow your procedure:

The definition of each construct and the source of the items (an existing scale, or one you created)
The sample size and how missing values were handled (for example, only complete cases were used)
The estimation method of the factor analysis (such as principal axis factoring), the rotation (promax), and the basis for the number of factors
The reverse-keyed items
The number of items and the alpha of each subscale
How the subscales were built (the simple mean of the items)

title: From survey items to a scale, then on to regression and QCA: a step-by-step guide
section: The whole procedure in a few words
text:
The whole procedure in a few words
A standard practical procedure has the following 11 stages. Steps 1 to 7 of this article rearrange these stages, except CFA (8) and SEM (11), in the order of building a scale (with a check of reverse-keyed items added).

Define the construct from prior research
Prepare several questionnaire items for each construct
Hold in advance a theoretical expectation of “which item measures which construct”
Use EFA to examine, in an exploratory way, whether that expectation is consistent with the actual data structure
Examine the items from both theoretical and statistical viewpoints
Check internal consistency with Cronbach’s alpha (and McDonald’s omega if needed)
Build subscales by simple means
Verify the measurement structure further with CFA, if needed
Use the subscales in regression and similar analyses
In QCA, calibrate the subscales and use them
If the structure among latent variables is itself the research aim, consider SEM

The most important point is not “collect data and then look for meaning by factor analysis,” but “define the meaning from theory, and use factor analysis to examine, in an exploratory way, whether that meaning also holds in the data.”
\[
\text{theory} \rightarrow \text{construct} \rightarrow \text{items} \rightarrow \text{examination of the measurement structure} \rightarrow \text{scaling} \rightarrow \text{hypothesis tests by regression, QCA, etc.}
\]
You do not need to decide mechanically that “we use constructs, so we use SEM.” What matters is that the research question, the theory, the measurement, the way of building scales, and the method of analysis are consistent with one another.
This article does not cover why you might not use SEM, or how SEM compares. I plan to write about that in a separate article (Notes).

title: From survey items to a scale, then on to regression and QCA: a step-by-step guide
text:
What to read next
The subscales you built in this article can also be used in QCA. While regression looks at the average association when the other variables are held constant, QCA looks for which combinations of conditions lead to the outcome. ThSQCA is an R package that shows how those combinations change when you move the target level (the threshold) of the outcome.

Why QCA suits decision-making: looking for “recipes” instead of single effects

ThSQCA for beginners, part 1: your first threshold sweep
